tips.title: Four kinds: bacteria, viruses, fungi, protists
tips.body: Know one named disease for each. Antibiotics kill **bacteria** only, and never viruses, which is why they do nothing for a cold.

tips.title: Communicable means it can be passed on
tips.body: **Communicable** diseases are caused by pathogens and spread from person to person. **Non-communicable** ones, such as heart disease or cancer, cannot be caught. That single test sorts any example.

tips.title: Name the control and say why it works
tips.body: "Use nets" is half an answer. "Use nets **so mosquitoes cannot reach people at night, breaking the transmission route**" is the mark. Every control needs its mechanism.

tips.title: Name the kind of pathogen first
tips.body: Deciding **bacterium, virus, fungus or protist** before anything else settles most of the answer: it rules antibiotics in or out, and it usually points at the route of transmission too. One word at the start saves picking your way through the biology later.

why.matters:
A pathogen has to **get to you**, and that is the weak point. You cannot usually stop an organism reproducing inside someone, but you can very often stop it arriving — and almost everything public health has ever achieved is that idea.

So the useful question about any infection is not *what does it do* but **how does it travel**. Name the route and the control follows, even for a disease you have never heard of, which is exactly what the exam asks you to do.

examples.title: Why a net beats a medicine
examples.body:
Malaria is caused by a protist, and the protist cannot walk. It needs a **mosquito** to carry it from one person to another, so a net over a bed at night breaks the chain without touching the pathogen at all.

Every control on the specification works that way. Cholera travels in water, so you treat the water. Tuberculosis travels in the air, so you ventilate the room and isolate the patient. Tie the control to the **route** and the answer is complete; give the control alone and it is half of one.

visual.alt: A table of three diseases with the route each uses and the control that cuts it: cholera in water treated at the supply, malaria by mosquito bite stopped with nets and drainage, and tuberculosis in the air met with ventilation

examples.title: Why a cold sore comes back years later
examples.body:
A virus cannot reproduce on its own; it has to get inside a cell and use it. Usually that is the **lytic** pathway: inject the genetic material, make hundreds of copies, burst the cell, and symptoms follow.

The textbook **lysogenic** pathway is different: the viral genetic material is **inserted into the host cell's own DNA** and lies dormant, copied each time the cell divides, until a trigger switches it to the lytic pathway.

The cold sore virus shows the same idea of lying dormant, by a slightly different route. After the first infection it hides in the **nerve cells** that supply the lip. Nerve cells do not divide, and the virus's DNA stays in the nucleus as a separate loop rather than being inserted into the host's DNA. It does nothing until something, such as another illness, stress or strong sunlight, reactivates it — which is why a cold sore reappears without anyone re-infecting you.

visual.alt: A flow chart of the two viral pathways: a virus enters a cell and either takes the lytic pathway, making copies and bursting the cell so symptoms follow, or the lysogenic pathway, where the genetic material lies dormant

examples.title: Why one illness opens the door to another
examples.body:
People with HIV often die of tuberculosis, and the connection is not a coincidence — it is a chain you can write down, which is exactly what an *explain* question wants.

HIV infects and destroys **lymphocytes**. Fewer lymphocytes means a weaker immune response. A weaker response means a pathogen that a healthy body would have contained is not contained. So a second infection takes hold that would otherwise never have caused illness. Each link is a mark, and the conclusion on its own is worth almost nothing.

visual.alt: A flow chart of one disease opening the door to another: an HIV infection destroys lymphocytes, the immune response weakens, and a second disease that a healthy body would have contained takes hold

steps.title: What health actually is
steps.body:
The **World Health Organization** (WHO) defines health as *a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity*.

That definition is wider than most people expect. Someone with no disease at all can still be unhealthy: lonely, anxious, or without enough food. And someone with a well-managed condition, such as asthma, can be healthy.

A **disease** is a condition that stops part of the body working properly. The rest of this unit is about what causes diseases, how they spread, how the body fights them, and how medicines are made to help.

steps.title: Communicable and non-communicable
steps.body:
**Communicable** diseases are caused by **pathogens** and can be passed from one person, animal or plant to another: cholera, tuberculosis, malaria.

**Non-communicable** diseases cannot be passed on: coronary heart disease, most cancers, type 2 diabetes. They usually come from a mix of factors, such as genes and lifestyle, and they are the subject of the last topic in this unit.

The two are linked. **Having one disease can make you more likely to get another.** HIV destroys white blood cells, so the immune system is weakened and infections such as tuberculosis take hold. Being malnourished weakens the body in the same way. This is why a disease in one part of a population can drive others up with it.

steps.title: Four kinds of pathogen
steps.body:
A **pathogen** is a microorganism that causes disease. There are four kinds on the specification, and each named disease belongs to one of them — learn them as pairs.

- **Bacteria**: single cells with no nucleus. Many release toxins. *Cholera, tuberculosis, stomach ulcers (Helicobacter), Chlamydia.*
- **Viruses**: not cells at all — genetic material in a protein coat. They can only reproduce inside a host cell. *HIV, Ebola.*
- **Fungi**: some are single cells, others grow threads through tissue; many spread by spores. *Chalara ash dieback.*
- **Protists**: single cells with a nucleus. *Malaria.*

The kind of pathogen matters later: **antibiotics only work on bacteria**, which is why they are useless against HIV.

steps.title: How they spread, and how to stop them
steps.body:
Every control measure works the same way: **find the route the pathogen uses, and cut it**. That is the sentence to carry into every question on this.

- **Water** (cholera): clean drinking water and treated sewage.
- **Airborne** (tuberculosis, Chalara): for TB, ventilation, covering coughs, isolating patients and the BCG vaccine; for Chalara, removing and burning infected trees and limiting the movement of ash plants.
- **Animal vectors** (malaria): a **vector** carries a pathogen between hosts. Stop the mosquito with nets, insecticide and draining standing water.
- *(Biology only.)* **Oral transmission** (stomach ulcers caused by *Helicobacter*): hygiene, and safe food and water.
- *(Biology only.)* **Body fluids** (Ebola): isolating patients, protective clothing, safe burial.

steps.title: Spotting and identifying plant disease
steps.body:
*(Higher tier, Biology only.)* Before a plant disease can be controlled, it has to be **detected** and the cause **identified**. That is done in two places.

**In the field**
- **Observe the symptoms**: spots or patches on leaves, discoloured or wilting leaves, stunted growth, rotting, unusual growths, or visible pests.
- **Look at the distribution**: map which plants are affected. A pathogen tends to spread outwards from where it started, while a pattern that follows the land — the wettest corner, one soil type — points to a cause in the environment.
- **Eliminate environmental causes**: frost, waterlogging and a shortage of minerals in the soil can all produce similar symptoms, so rule them out.

**In the lab**
- **Diagnostic testing** identifies the pathogen itself: examining samples under a microscope, growing the microorganism, or using a DNA test or a kit containing antibodies that bind only to that pathogen.

steps.title: Viruses: the lytic and lysogenic pathways
steps.body:
*(Biology only.)* A virus cannot reproduce on its own; it has to use a host cell. There are two ways it can go.

**The lytic pathway.** The virus **attaches** to a cell and **injects** its genetic material. The cell is taken over: it **copies** the viral genetic material and makes viral proteins, which **assemble** into new viruses. Then the cell **bursts** — *lysis* — releasing them to infect more cells.

**The lysogenic pathway.** The viral genetic material is **inserted into the host's DNA**. Every time the cell divides, the viral genes are copied too, so they spread through new cells without doing any damage. They lie **dormant** until a trigger switches them into the lytic pathway.

This is why some viral infections cause symptoms long after the person was infected.

steps.title: Sexually transmitted infections
steps.body:
**Sexually transmitted infections** (STIs) are spread by sexual contact. The specification names two, and they are different kinds of pathogen, which matters for treatment.

**Chlamydia** is a **bacterium**. It often causes no symptoms, so people pass it on without knowing, and it can lead to infertility. Because it is a bacterium, it can be cured with **antibiotics**.

**HIV** is a **virus**. As well as sex, it spreads through **blood** — shared needles, and from mother to baby. Antibiotics do not work on it, but **antiretroviral drugs** reduce the amount of virus.

Reducing spread: **condoms** for both; **screening** so infected people are found and treated; and for HIV, not sharing needles and screening donated blood.

visuals.alt: A table comparing Chlamydia and HIV: pathogen, how each spreads, treatment and how spread is reduced

check.prompt: Which measure reduces the spread of both Chlamydia and HIV?
check.solution: **Condoms** stop the transfer of body fluids during sex, which is how both spread. Antibiotics treat only Chlamydia.

steps.title: Going deeper: routes, chains and unfamiliar diseases
steps.body:
Three habits mark out the top answers in this topic.

**Tie every control to the route.** *Use nets* earns less than *use nets, so mosquitoes cannot bite and pass on the protist*. The examiner wants to see that you know **why** the measure works.

**Write chains, not lists, for *explain* questions.** Why does HIV make TB more likely? Destroys white blood cells → immune system weakened → TB bacteria not destroyed. Each link follows from the last.

**Transfer to the unfamiliar.** The harder questions give a disease you have not met — spread by ticks, by fleas, by shared cups. Classify the route, then reach for the control you would use for the named disease with the same route.

And for the Biology-only virus lifecycle: know the **order** of the lytic pathway, and that the lysogenic pathway explains **delayed** symptoms.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Health** (WHO): complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease.
- **Communicable** diseases are caused by pathogens and spread; **non-communicable** ones do not.
- **One disease can raise the risk of another**: HIV destroys white blood cells, weakening the immune system, so TB takes hold.
- **Four pathogens**: bacteria, viruses, fungi, protists. Learn each named disease with its pathogen.
- **Named infections**: cholera (bacterium, diarrhoea), tuberculosis (bacterium, lung damage), Chalara (fungus, leaf loss and bark lesions), malaria (protist, blood and liver), HIV (virus, white blood cells, AIDS), stomach ulcers (*Helicobacter*), Ebola (virus, haemorrhagic fever).
- **Routes**: water, airborne, animal vectors, oral transmission, body fluids. **The control always cuts the route.**
- **Viruses**: lytic — attach, inject, copy, assemble, burst; lysogenic — inserted into host DNA, dormant, later lytic.
- **Plant disease** is detected in the field (symptoms, distribution, ruling out environmental causes) and identified in the lab by diagnostic testing.
- **STIs**: Chlamydia (bacterium, antibiotics) and HIV (virus, antiretrovirals); condoms and screening for both.

questions.prompt: Explain how the spread of malaria can be reduced.
questions.solution: Two chains, because malaria has a vector and a pathogen. Treat people: antimalarial drugs kill the protist, so infected people cannot pass it on when bitten.

questions.modelAnswer: Malaria is spread by mosquitoes, so one way is to stop people being bitten: sleeping under nets treated with insecticide means infected mosquitoes cannot reach them, so fewer people are infected. Draining standing water removes the places where mosquitoes lay their eggs, so there are fewer mosquitoes to carry the protist. Treating infected people with antimalarial drugs kills the protist in their blood, so a mosquito that bites them cannot pick it up and pass it on.

questions.modelAnswer: Both are communicable diseases, but they spread in very different ways. Cholera bacteria are carried in **water** contaminated with infected faeces, whereas the Ebola virus passes directly through the **body fluids** of infected people, such as blood or vomit. Because of that, the controls differ. Cholera is reduced by providing **clean drinking water** and **treating sewage**, which breaks the route for a whole community at once. Ebola is reduced by **isolating** patients, giving carers **protective clothing**, and burying the dead safely, all of which stop contact with body fluids. In each case the control works by cutting the particular route the pathogen uses.

questions.prompt: In a made-up study, 60 of 2000 people living with HIV developed tuberculosis in one year, compared with 30 of 20 000 people without HIV. How many times more likely was a person with HIV to develop tuberculosis?

finds the rate without HIV, 0.15% or 0.0015

questions.prompt: Which disease is caused by a virus and causes haemorrhagic fever?
questions.solution: **Ebola.** Ebola is a virus spread in body fluids, and it causes haemorrhagic fever, a fever with bleeding. Cholera is a bacterium that causes diarrhoea, malaria is a protist that damages the blood and liver, and Chlamydia is a bacterium spread by sexual contact.

markScheme.description: Ebola

options: Cholera
Malaria
Chlamydia
Ebola

questions.prompt: A student says that a disease must be non-communicable because tests show it is not caused by bacteria. Why is this reasoning wrong?
questions.solution: **Bacteria are only one of four kinds of pathogen.** A communicable disease is one caused by a pathogen and passed from one organism to another, and pathogens include viruses, fungi and protists as well as bacteria: HIV and Ebola are viruses, Chalara ash dieback is a fungus and malaria is a protist. Ruling out bacteria rules out one kind of pathogen, not all of them. Non-communicable diseases are not caused by any pathogen, and how severe a disease is has nothing to do with whether it can be passed on.

markScheme.description: communicable diseases can be caused by viruses, fungi and protists, not only bacteria

options: Non-communicable diseases are the ones caused by bacteria, so this disease must be communicable
Communicable diseases can be caused by viruses, fungi and protists, not only by bacteria
A disease can only be classed as non-communicable once every kind of bacterium has been tested for
Whether a disease is communicable depends on how severe it is, not on what causes it

questions.prompt: Chalara ash dieback is a fungus that causes ash trees to lose their leaves and develop lesions in the bark. Foresters find that ash trees with Chalara are often killed by a second fungus that grows in from the soil, which healthy ash trees usually resist. Which explanation best fits these observations?
questions.solution: **The first disease weakens the tree's defences, so the second can take hold.** This is the same idea as HIV leading to tuberculosis, applied to a plant. The lesions break the bark, which is the tree's physical barrier against pathogens, giving the second fungus a way in. Losing leaves means less photosynthesis, so the tree has less glucose for growth, repair and the chemicals it uses to fight infection. A weakened tree is more susceptible to a disease it would normally resist. Chalara does not turn into another fungus, it is spread by the wind and not by an insect, and the second fungus grows from the soil, so it does not need light on the bark.

markScheme.description: lesions break the physical barrier and leaf loss cuts the glucose for defence, so the tree is more susceptible

options: Chalara changes into the second fungus once all the leaves have fallen, so the two diseases are really the same infection at two stages
The second fungus needs light to reach the bark, and only a tree that has lost its leaves lets enough light through for it to grow
The bark lesions break the tree's physical barrier and leaf loss cuts its glucose supply, so a weakened tree cannot resist the second fungus
Both fungi are carried by the same insect vector, so any tree that has been infected with one must have been infected with the other

questions.prompt: A farmer finds wheat plants with yellow, stunted leaves. The affected plants form a patch that started in one corner of the field and has grown wider every week. The healthy plants in the rest of the field grow in the same soil, with the same drainage and the same fertiliser. What does the distribution suggest, and what should the farmer do next?
questions.solution: **A pathogen spreading from where it started, so send samples for diagnostic testing.** Distribution analysis is one of the ways of detecting plant disease in the field. A patch that spreads outwards from a starting point, week by week, is the pattern of a pathogen passing from plant to plant. The environmental causes that produce similar symptoms have been eliminated: the healthy plants share the same soil, drainage and fertiliser, so a shortage of minerals, waterlogging or frost would have affected the whole field or followed the lie of the land, and none of them moves from plant to plant. Observing the symptoms and the distribution says there is probably a pathogen; only diagnostic testing in the lab, for example a DNA test or an antibody kit, identifies which one.

markScheme.description: a pathogen spreading from its starting point; diagnostic testing to identify it

options: A shortage of a mineral in the soil, because a deficiency passes from plant to plant across a field over several weeks
Frost damage, because frost always strikes one corner of a field first and then spreads across it week by week
A pathogen is spreading outwards from where it started, so samples should go for diagnostic testing to identify it
An environmental cause, because the affected and the healthy plants are growing in exactly the same soil

questions.prompt: Name the organisation whose definition of health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.
questions.solution: **The World Health Organization (WHO).** Its definition has three parts, physical, mental and social well-being, and all three must be complete. A person with no disease who is lonely or anxious is not healthy by this definition.

markScheme.description: World Health Organization / WHO

questions.prompt: Chlamydia is a sexually transmitted infection caused by a bacterium. It often causes no symptoms, so infected people can pass it on without knowing. A screening programme tested 2500 young people who had no symptoms, and 175 of them tested positive. Calculate the percentage of the people tested who were infected.
questions.solution: Percentage infected $= \dfrac{175}{2500} \times 100 = 7$%. Every one of these 175 people felt well, so without the test they would not have known they were infected and could have passed the bacterium on through unprotected sex. Screening finds them so they can be treated with antibiotics, which works because Chlamydia is a bacterium, and condoms stop the bacterium passing between partners in the meantime.

markScheme.description: divides 175 by 2500 and multiplies by 100

questions.prompt: A village has 12 000 people. In one year it recorded 40 cases of malaria for every 1000 people. Insecticide-treated bed nets were then given to every household, and in the following year 288 cases of malaria were recorded in the whole village. Calculate the percentage decrease in the number of cases per 1000 people.
questions.skill: evaluating a control measure from case data
questions.solution: First put both years on the same footing. The village is $12\,000 \div 1000 = 12$ lots of 1000 people, so the second year's rate is $\dfrac{288}{12} = 24$ cases per 1000. The fall is $40 - 24 = 16$ per 1000, and $\dfrac{16}{40} \times 100 = 40$%. (Checking the other way: 40 per 1000 in a village of 12 000 is $40 \times 12 = 480$ cases, and $\dfrac{480 - 288}{480} \times 100 = 40$%.) The nets work because malaria is spread by a mosquito vector: fewer bites, so fewer people receive the protist.

markScheme.description: converts 288 cases in 12 000 people to 24 per 1000 (or 40 per 1000 to 480 cases)
divides the fall by the original figure: 16/40 or 192/480

questions.prompt: Patients with tuberculosis are nursed in well-ventilated rooms and asked to cover their mouths when they cough. Explain why these two measures reduce the spread of tuberculosis.
questions.skill: reducing the spread of an airborne pathogen
questions.solution: Tuberculosis is caused by a **bacterium** that is **airborne**: when an infected person coughs or sneezes, the bacteria leave the lungs in droplets, and other people are infected by breathing those droplets in. **Covering the mouth** traps the droplets before they reach the air that others breathe. **Ventilation** moves fresh air through the room and carries infected droplets away, so the air contains far fewer bacteria for anyone else to inhale.

markScheme.description: the bacteria are airborne, carried in droplets released by coughing and breathed in by others
covering the mouth traps the droplets so they do not reach the air others breathe
ventilation carries the droplets away so fewer bacteria are in the air to be inhaled

criteria.text: States that the tuberculosis bacteria are airborne: they leave the lungs in droplets when the patient coughs and infect others who breathe them in
Explains that covering the mouth traps the droplets so they do not reach the air that other people breathe
Explains that ventilation moves fresh air through the room and carries the droplets away, so fewer bacteria remain in the air to be inhaled

questions.modelAnswer: Tuberculosis is caused by a bacterium that spreads through the air. When a patient coughs or sneezes, bacteria from the damaged lungs are carried out in tiny droplets, and anyone who breathes those droplets in can be infected. Covering the mouth when coughing traps the droplets in a hand or tissue, so most of the bacteria never reach the air that other people in the room are breathing. Good ventilation keeps fresh air moving through the room and carries any droplets that do escape out of it, so the air contains far fewer bacteria and the chance that a nurse or visitor inhales enough to become infected is much lower. Both measures work for the same reason: the pathogen travels by air, so the controls cut the number of bacteria in the air.

questions.prompt: A virus infects a cell and enters the lysogenic pathway. Over the following weeks the number of cells carrying the viral genetic material rises steadily, yet no new virus particles are released and the person has no symptoms. Explain these observations.
questions.solution: In the **lysogenic pathway** the viral genetic material is **inserted into the host cell's DNA** instead of being used straight away to make new viruses. Each time the host cell divides, it copies all of its DNA, including the viral genes, so **both daughter cells carry the virus**; that is why the number of infected cells rises with every division without any virus being released. The viral genes stay **dormant**: no viral proteins are made, no new virus particles are assembled and no cell bursts (lysis), so there is nothing to cause symptoms until a trigger switches the virus into the lytic pathway.

markScheme.description: the viral genetic material is inserted into the host cell's DNA
when the host cell divides the viral genes are copied and passed to both daughter cells, so infected cells increase
the viral genes are dormant: no viral proteins or particles are made and no lysis, so no symptoms until a trigger starts the lytic pathway

criteria.text: States that in the lysogenic pathway the viral genetic material is inserted into the host cell's own DNA
Explains that each time the host cell divides its DNA is copied, including the viral genes, so both daughter cells carry the virus and the number of infected cells rises

Explains that the viral genes stay dormant, so no viral proteins or new particles are made and no cell bursts, which is why there are no symptoms until a trigger switches the virus to the lytic pathway

questions.modelAnswer: In the lysogenic pathway the virus does not take over the cell straight away. Its genetic material is inserted into the host cell's own DNA, where it sits as part of the cell's genome. A cell dividing by mitosis copies all of its DNA before it divides, and the viral genes are copied along with everything else, so each daughter cell receives a copy. Every round of division therefore doubles the number of cells carrying the virus, which is why the count rises steadily week after week even though no virus has left any cell. While the viral genes are part of the host DNA they are dormant: the cell does not read them to make viral proteins, no new virus particles are assembled, and the cell is not destroyed by lysis. Symptoms come from cells being damaged and burst, so a dormant virus produces none. Only when a trigger, such as stress or another infection, switches the viral genes into the lytic pathway does the cell begin making and releasing new viruses, and that can be years after the original infection.

questions.prompt: After a flood, thousands of people are living in a relief camp. The tents are crowded, drinking water is taken from a river, and pools of standing water lie between the tents. Explain why outbreaks of cholera, tuberculosis and malaria are all more likely in the camp than in an ordinary town, and describe one measure for each disease that would reduce its spread.
questions.skill: linking the route of spread to the control
questions.solution: The three diseases have three different routes, and each condition in the camp opens one of them. **Cholera** is a bacterium spread in **water**; the river is also where waste ends up, so people drink water contaminated with the bacteria from the diarrhoea of those already infected. Control: boil or chlorinate drinking water, or bring in a clean supply, and keep latrines away from the river. **Tuberculosis** is a bacterium that is **airborne**, in droplets coughed out by an infected person; in crowded tents many people breathe the same air, so the droplets reach many more people. Control: reduce crowding and improve ventilation, and isolate and treat anyone with symptoms. **Malaria** is a protist carried by a **mosquito vector**; mosquitoes breed in standing water, so the pools between the tents mean more mosquitoes and more bites. Control: drain the standing water, or give out insecticide-treated nets so people are not bitten while they sleep. In each case the measure works by blocking the route the pathogen uses.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): names the route of spread for one or two of the diseases, or lists control measures without linking them to the conditions in the camp

Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): links at least two diseases to the camp condition that favours them (contaminated river water, crowded tents, standing water) with a suitable control for each, with some gaps in the reasoning

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): for all three diseases, names the pathogen's route, explains how the specific camp condition increases spread by that route, and gives a control that blocks the route, in a clear chain of reasoning

criteria.text: Explains that cholera bacteria spread in water, and that river water used for drinking is contaminated by waste from infected people
Gives a control that blocks the water route: boiling or chlorinating drinking water, a clean supply, or latrines kept away from the river
Explains that tuberculosis bacteria are airborne in coughed-out droplets, and that crowded tents mean many people breathe the same air
Gives a control that blocks the airborne route: less crowding, better ventilation, or isolating and treating people with symptoms
Explains that the malaria protist is carried by a mosquito vector, and that mosquitoes breed in the standing water between the tents
Gives a control that blocks the vector route: draining the standing water, insecticide-treated nets, insecticide or repellent

questions.modelAnswer:
**Cholera** is caused by a bacterium that is spread in **water**. In the camp the river is the only source of drinking water, and with no proper sanitation the waste from people who already have cholera, which contains the bacteria from their diarrhoea, drains into the same river. Everyone who drinks from it swallows the bacteria, so one case quickly becomes an outbreak. The spread is reduced by making the drinking water safe: boiling or chlorinating it, bringing in a clean supply, and siting latrines well away from the river so the water is not contaminated in the first place.

**Tuberculosis** is caused by a bacterium that is **airborne**. When an infected person coughs, bacteria leave the lungs in droplets, and others are infected by breathing them in. In a crowded tent many people breathe the same small volume of air, close together and for many hours, so the droplets from one person reach far more people than they would in a house. The spread is reduced by cutting the number of bacteria in the air that others breathe: fewer people to a tent, good ventilation, and finding anyone with a persistent cough so they can be isolated and treated.

**Malaria** is caused by a protist that is carried from person to person by a **mosquito**, an animal vector. Mosquitoes lay their eggs in still water, so the pools of standing water between the tents are breeding sites, and more mosquitoes mean more bites and more chances for the protist to pass from an infected person to a healthy one. The spread is reduced by attacking the vector: draining or covering the standing water so the mosquitoes cannot breed, and giving every family insecticide-treated bed nets so they are not bitten at night, when the mosquitoes feed.

The three diseases are more likely for the same underlying reason. A pathogen has to travel, and the camp has removed the barriers that normally stand in the way of each route. The control in each case puts a barrier back on that route.

examTechnique.body:
Topic 5 is on Paper 1, and this part of it is a knowledge test before it is anything else: each named disease with its pathogen, its effect and its route. Learn the table until any one column gives you the other two, because questions routinely give one and ask for another.

The marks above the recall are for reasoning. A control measure scores when it is tied to the route it cuts. An *explain* answer scores when it is a chain in which each step follows from the last. And the hardest questions give a disease you have never met, where the method is to classify its route and apply the control you would use for a named disease with the same route.
examinerErrors: Calling a virus a bacterium, or suggesting antibiotics for HIV or Ebola. Antibiotics only work on bacteria.
Naming a control without saying why it works: *use nets* rather than *nets stop mosquitoes biting and passing on the protist*.
Mixing up the routes: cholera is water-borne, tuberculosis airborne, Ebola through body fluids.
Describing malaria as a bacterial or viral disease. It is caused by a protist, carried by a mosquito vector.
Explaining why HIV makes TB likely without the middle link: that the immune system is weakened because white blood cells are destroyed.
Confusing the lytic and lysogenic pathways. Lytic ends with the cell bursting; lysogenic inserts viral genes into the host DNA, where they lie dormant.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer knows every named disease across all three columns — pathogen, effect, route — without hesitation. It ties each control measure to the route it breaks, writes explanations as chains in which each link causes the next, and handles an unfamiliar disease by classifying its route and reasoning from the named disease that shares it. On viruses it gives the lytic pathway in order and uses the lysogenic pathway to explain symptoms that appear long after infection.
